opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think stepping outside your comfort zone matters mostly because the comfort zone is where you stop learning. When you're doing something you already know how to do well, you're mostly executing. That has value, but you're not building new mental models.

Looking back on my own path, the moments that taught me the most were the ones where I didn't fully know what I was doing. Going from academic research, where you care about whether an idea is elegant and whether the paper is solid, to building infrastructure that thousands of engineers depend on was a big shift. Suddenly the questions were about reliability, scale, and how people actually use the tool, not just whether the algorithm is clever. Later, moving from a big company into starting something of my own was another jump. In a large organization there's a lot of structure around you. When you start a company, you're figuring out product, hiring, fundraising, and talking to customers, all at once, and many of those things you've never done before.

Those transitions are uncomfortable. You feel slow, you make mistakes, and sometimes you question whether you belong there. But that discomfort is a signal that you're stretching. After a while, the thing that felt foreign becomes part of your toolkit, and you start seeing connections across domains that you couldn't see before. A lot of good ideas in AI came from people who understood both the research side and the systems or engineering side, and you only get that combination by being willing to step into the area you're not an expert in.

The other part is humility. When you're outside your comfort zone, you have to listen more, ask naive questions, and learn from people who know more than you. I think that attitude is healthy for anyone, especially in a field moving as fast as AI, where what you're comfortable with today may be outdated in a year or two. So for me, it's less about seeking discomfort for its own sake and more about recognizing that growth almost always lives just past the edge of what feels easy.

r001.rationale: The response says growth comes from taking on unfamiliar challenges and learning beyond one’s existing expertise, with examples of useful work across research, infrastructure, and founding a company.

r002.rationale: It does not contrast control over one’s own code with frustration from depending on people in organizational work.

r003.rationale: It describes learning from product, hiring, fundraising, and customers, but does not say those experiences develop a perspective that outweighs technical advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that comfort zones are really good at hiding what you don't know. When I was doing research at Berkeley and building Caffe, I was very comfortable with the technical side: writing code, reading papers, benchmarking models. And I was pretty good at it. But that comfort also meant I had a very narrow view of what it actually takes to make technology matter in the world.

Then I went to Google, and later to Facebook, and then to Alibaba, and each time I was dropped into a situation where my old skills were necessary but nowhere near sufficient. At Facebook I had to think about how a framework like PyTorch and Caffe2 would be used by thousands of engineers I would never meet. At Alibaba I was suddenly responsible for a business unit, for cloud products, for people whose careers depended on decisions I made. None of that was in my comfort zone. I made a lot of mistakes.

But the thing is, you only discover your blind spots when you're forced to operate outside the area where your existing instincts work. Inside the comfort zone, your mental model and reality mostly agree, so you don't get much new information. Outside it, you get feedback constantly, and often it hurts. That feedback is the growth. You start to notice that the questions you thought were "soft," like how to communicate a technical trade-off to a non-technical person, or how to set priorities when everything looks urgent, are actually very hard problems with real structure to them.

Starting Lepton AI was probably the biggest step outside for me. As a founder you have no institutional cover. Nobody cares about your résumé when the product is down or a customer isn't paying. Every week there's a new category of problem I've never solved before. It's uncomfortable in a very literal sense, but I'd say I've learned more about myself and about how technology actually gets adopted in the last couple of years than in the previous ten combined.

So I don't think of leaving the comfort zone as a virtue in itself. It's more that it's the only reliable way I've found to keep learning once you've gotten reasonably good at something. If everything feels easy, you're probably not seeing the whole picture.

r001.rationale: The response presents leaving the comfort zone as a reliable way to keep learning and gives examples of taking on unfamiliar responsibilities beyond existing technical skills.

r002.rationale: It discusses organizational responsibilities and mistakes, but does not contrast control over one's own code with frustration at depending on other people.

r003.rationale: The response says technical skill alone gave a narrow view of what makes technology matter, and credits business, leadership, and adoption experience with developing a broader perspective.

astra-6.text:
I think stepping outside your comfort zone helps because it exposes the things you haven’t learned yet. When you’re doing something familiar, you know how to approach the problem, and you can become very efficient. But you may also stop questioning your assumptions.

When you enter an unfamiliar situation, you have to ask basic questions again, listen to other people, and accept that you won’t get everything right immediately. That can be uncomfortable, but it’s also how you develop new perspectives and skills.

For me, the important thing is to take on a challenge where you have something to learn. Over time, something that initially felt intimidating becomes something you can handle. Your comfort zone grows.

r001.rationale: It recommends taking on a challenge where one has something to learn, but does not say the work should be useful or lie outside one’s current competence.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss control over one’s own code or dependence on other people in organizational work.

r003.rationale: It mentions gaining perspectives and skills, but does not credit experience beyond technical work with making technical advantage less important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think stepping outside your comfort zone helps you discover where your assumptions stop working. When you do something familiar, you already know how to make progress. In a new environment, you have to ask questions, listen to other people, and become a beginner again. That can be uncomfortable, but it’s also where you learn a lot.

It doesn’t have to mean making a huge change all at once. You can take on a problem you haven’t solved before or work with people who think differently. Over time, those experiences build confidence—not because you know everything, but because you learn that you can adapt when you don’t.

r001.rationale: It recommends taking on a problem you haven’t solved before and describes learning and confidence gained from doing so.

r002.rationale: It does not compare control over one’s own code with the frustration of depending on others in organizational work.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss experience beyond technical work or weigh broader perspective against technical advantage.
